In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "From Gondwana to the Yellow Sea: evolutionary diversifications of true toads (Bufo sp.) in the Eastern Palearctic, and a revisit of species boundaries for Asian lineages" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and George Perry as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Jonathan J Fong (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission. Both reviewers found merit in your study, but also both of them found important shortcomings with the style of your writing, and with the amount of detail in some parts of the text. A successful revision will require that you change this, and the main text on the manuscript becomes more readable for general audiences, without losing the precision that specialist readers of eLife are looking for.

Essential revisions:

1) It seems we both had the same reading of the manuscript. It can be a great contribution, but the text is rather loaded with unnecessary details; messages are hidden in large tables; figures are nice, but many times just too busy to appreciate; and, a lot of very specific jargon is retained in most sentences. Thus, the reviewers suggest the authors to reorganize the manuscript in a text that is more hypothesis testing, less descriptive. One idea you can try is adding subsections that contain specific evolutionary/ecological hypotheses your manuscript addresses. Another way is through eliminating many sentences that describe numerical results, (analysis) model assumptions, and other sentences that do not say explicitly what they really want to say. For example, replace lines 332-334 (or the whole paragraph for that end) for the text closer to the frogs have different niches!. Finally, you can build longer appendices.

2) Please provide actual taxonomic accounts of the species, and justify properly new taxonomic changes. Lines 410-418. Not sure this paragraph is needed since you really did not provide taxonomic treatment of the species. Please include these changes in all sections of the manuscript.

3) On the reviewers added an annotated pdf with detailed suggestions. It is a combination of minor corrections to text, to issues about clarity and structure. Whenever possible, the reviewer has tried to provide some alternative approaches-they should be tried, but ultimately the reviewer trust the authors will decide what works best.Reviewer #1:

Summary: This paper looks at the evolution of toad species in the family Bufonidae at two different geographic scales: global and regional in Asia. On the global scale, the authors verify many of the previously known patterns in Bufonidae, such as Asian Bufo being a result of a single event. The regional scale is where much of the new work comes in. On the regional scale, the authors take an exhaustive approach to clarify the systematics of Bufo, using phylogenetic analyses, divergence dating, structure analysis, evaluation of migration and introgression, ecological niche modelling. Through this integrative approach, the authors are able to provide a good assessment of the Bufo species present in Asia, as well as hypotheses for the speciation, and taxonomic revision.

Strengths: The goals are clear, analyses appropriate and thorough, and the results support their discussion. The authors have worked hard to use applicable analyses and test assumptions/priors by modifying them. The manuscript is generally well written-I especially liked the introduction and discussion, with most of it being very clear and straightforward.

Weaknesses: Abstract could be revised to better reflect what the manuscript is about-currently the abstract undersells what they are doing. The analyses are thorough, but the authors could do a better job simplifying and interpreting the results. I think many of the tests of the assumptions/priors could be quickly discussed (e.g. all of our tests point towards the same result) and not distract from their results. A clearer, more straightforward explanation of the results would help clarify the interesting points. The figures are pretty and must have taken a lot of work, but are currently too complicated. A figure should be easily and quickly understood, even without reading the manuscript-currently most of the figures would need at least 30 minutes to fully understand (if possible). As with the results, simplification would benefit the manuscript. I have provided some suggestions, but ultimately it will need to be tested. Some general suggestions for the writing-there are lots of terms (names, regions) and it would help if the terms were reduced and consistent across sections of the paper. Also, with names, the author should be aware that the formatting of the manuscript is a bit different (with the methods at the end). As a result, some of the names suddenly appear for the first time in the results (e.g. many of the B. g subspecies, B. sachalinensis [which is not a commonly used or known name]). I do not know the proper format, but I was actually confused about this because you have two B. s. species (B. sachalinensis and B. stejnegeri). For much of the paper, I didn't know which the abbreviation was referring to. The authors need to be careful to follow proper naming protocol as well as stay consistent throughout the paper.

Appraisal: Yes, the authors achieved their aims and the results support their conclusions.

Impact: For future phylogenetic studies, this paper provides a good foundation on a suite of potential analyses that can be performed, and their uses. For biogeographic studies in Eurasia and East Asia (especially Northeast Asia), this study provides a nice study which to compare to. For people interested in Asian Bufo species, this paper provides a good synthesis and revision of the species in the region There have been occasional studies comparing the species that often have conflicting results (e.g. a single or multiple species). This study combines multiple data types (genetics, geography, niche, geology) to try to clarify the situation. It is a reasonable conclusion-don't know if it is the "true" answer, but it is a great synthesis of what we currently know, and future researchers can use as a comparison point.Reviewer #2:

Othman et al., merge a large number of analyses to test for phytogeographic reconstruction of Bufo toads across East Asia. To do so they resolve both (1) the history of the genus since Gondwana split (reconstructing the evolution of the clade in the Americas, North Africa, and Eurasia) and (2) supply Eastern Palearctic reconstructions of 'local' Bufo species to test among competing hypotheses of regional Miocene radiations.

The strengths of the paper reside in the extreme detail, the inclusive nature of the ideas, and insightful reconstructions of the evolutionary history of these Bufo species, as supported by a large and complementary set of analyses. The weaknesses are actually the same! as the text is rather difficult to follow (specially for non-specialists), the main messages are hidden among many pages of (numerical) results, and large amounts of information are simplified in impressive, but many times difficult, figures. The large number of analyses do not really help to retain the take-home message as readers would have to be knowledgeable in many different methodologies to fully understand the whole picture. One further weakness is the taxonomic treatment of the species. In my opinion, taxonomic changes should be done in a more traditional way, justifying, species by species, the changes proposed in a proper and formal way. In a manuscript like this one, authors should marry the changes they propose since the beginning! This way older names are not perpetuated by the same manuscript that is trying to resolve them. Resolving taxonomy means that manuscript/figures/tables should be devoid of such names as B. sachalinensis spp B. sachalinensis sachalinensis, complexes, and other terminology.

results.result: The fossilized birth-death dating analysis established divergence times for Holarctic bufonids, showing that bufonids first diverged into American and African-Eurasian clades following the split of West Gondwana, with subsequent radiations occurring from the Early Oligocene to Middle Miocene. The Palearctic Bufo split into Western and Eastern clades around 14.49 Mya, with the Asian Bufo clade emerging around 9.99 Mya.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C65 present a comprehensive dating analysis using fossilized birth-death methods with fossil calibrations. The results are internally consistent, with the alternative Yule model (C65) corroborating the main findings. The dating estimates are supported by fossil evidence (Table 1, Figure 2) and include credible intervals (HPD 95%). The temporal framework is coherent across multiple lineages.

results.result: The split between Western and Eastern Palearctic Bufo occurred during the Middle Miocene (c. 14.49-10.00 Mya) and temporally matches with the maximum dust outflows in Central Asian deserts (c. 15.00-13.00 Mya), supporting the hypothesis that Central Asian desertification drove the segregation of these lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C58, C133, C144, and C145 establish a temporal correlation between the Bufo divergence and Central Asian desertification. The dating estimates (Table 1, Figure 2) show overlap between the divergence time (14.49 Mya) and the period of maximum dust outflows (15.00-13.00 Mya) cited from Guo et al., 2002. While temporal correlation does not prove causation, the consistency across multiple analyses and the geological context provide strong support for this biogeographic hypothesis.

results.result: Nested sampling analyses identified geological events (Model C) as the best predictor of Eastern Palearctic Bufo topology, with higher likelihood than models based on life history, morphology, or distributional range. The analysis rejected the monophyly of 'Torrentophryne' and supported three well-resolved monophyletic clades: Bufotes, Western Palearctic Bufo, and Eastern Palearctic Bufo.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 and C153-C157 present a model selection analysis using nested sampling with clear ranking of alternative hypotheses. Model C (geological events) received the highest MLE value (Supplementary file 1C, Figure 3), and the topology is well-supported with high posterior probabilities (PP: 1.0 for Bufotes and Eastern Palearctic Bufo; PP: 0.90 for Western Palearctic Bufo). The rejection of 'Torrentophryne' monophyly is corroborated by previous studies (Liu et al., 2000; Pyron and Wiens, 2011). The analysis appropriately tests multiple competing hypotheses.

results.result: Population genetic analyses of mtDNA and nuDNA revealed distinct patterns: mtDNA showed 98 haplotypes with 55.48% of variance among clades and high fixation indices (FST=0.78), while nuDNA showed high haplotype diversity (Hd=0.972) but low correlation between geographic and genetic distance for both markers.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C77 present standard population genetic statistics (AMOVA, fixation indices, Mantel tests) with appropriate sample sizes and statistical measures. The AMOVA results (Supplementary file 1E) show clear hierarchical structure, and the fixation indices indicate strong differentiation among clades. The negative correlation for mtDNA (r=-0.059) and low positive correlation for nuDNA (r=0.072) suggest factors other than isolation by distance are shaping genetic structure, which is consistent with the study's emphasis on geological events and dispersal.

results.result: Mitochondrial and nuclear phylogenies showed discordant topologies, particularly in the placement of B. gargarizans populations and the relationships among B. bankorensis, B. andrewsi, and Japanese Bufo subspecies. The D-statistic analysis (D=1.0) indicated that introgression, in addition to incomplete lineage sorting and differential evolutionary rates, contributed to this mitonuclear discordance.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 and C147-C152 document phylogenetic discordance with clear evidence from Figure 4 and Table 2. The D-statistic value of 1.0 (C87, C150) with unsymmetrical ABBA-BABA frequencies provides statistical support for introgression. The interpretation considers multiple explanations (differential evolutionary rates, incomplete lineage sorting, introgression) and cites relevant literature (San Mauro et al., 2004; Bell and Irian, 2019; Yu et al., 2014). However, the D-statistic analysis could benefit from additional details about the specific populations tested and the statistical significance of the deviation from equal frequencies.

results.result: Molecular dating and ancestral range reconstruction revealed that East Asian Bufo diversified from the Early to Late Miocene (c. 14.20 Mya), with vicariance events isolating Japanese Bufo (c. 8.23 Mya) and high-altitude clades (B. tibetanus, B. andrewsi, B. gargarizans; c. 11.32 Mya), followed by Plio-Pleistocene radiations within the B. gargarizans complex and dispersal to septentrional East Asia.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C102 and C158-C165 present a comprehensive temporal framework for East Asian Bufo diversification based on mtDNA and nuDNA dating (Table 3, Figure 5). The dates are consistent with geological events (QTP orogenesis, Japanese Archipelago drift) and previous studies (Igawa et al., 2006; Macey et al., 1998; Fong et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2017). The analysis includes credible intervals (HPD 95%) and tests multiple tree priors. The integration of dating with ancestral range reconstruction (BBM-DIVA) provides a coherent biogeographic narrative. Minor concern: some dates differ slightly from previous estimates, but the authors acknowledge and explain these differences.

results.result: Population dynamics analyses using neutrality tests and Bayesian Skyline Plots showed that the Amur River Basin clade (B. s. sachalinensis) underwent recent population expansion starting c. 0.48 Mya, while the southwestern Yellow Sea clade (B. gargarizans) showed consistent decline since c. 0.55 Mya, supporting the hypothesis of ice-age refugia and differential responses to glaciation.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 and C169 present population dynamics analyses with appropriate statistical tests (Tajima's D, Fu's Fs) showing significant negative values for the Amur River Basin clade (Supplementary file 1D), and Bayesian Skyline Plots (Figure 6) with credible intervals and likelihood values. The contrasting patterns between the two clades (expansion vs. decline) are clearly demonstrated and consistent with the ice-age refugia hypothesis. The effective population size trajectories are well-documented with HPD intervals.

results.result: Ecological niche modeling demonstrated significant niche segregation between B. gargarizans and B. sachalinensis, with both models showing high predictive performance (AUC >0.92, TSS >0.67). Niche overlap statistics (I=0.4198, D=0.1566) were significantly lower than null expectations (p<0.0001), with minimum temperatures being key factors differentiating the niches.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 and C173-C174 present robust ecological niche modeling with appropriate validation metrics (AUC, TSS) indicating good model performance. The niche overlap analysis includes a null model comparison with statistical significance testing, showing that the observed overlap is significantly less than expected by chance. The identification of temperature variables (BIO 6 and 11) as key differentiating factors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) is supported by response curves. The analysis appropriately addresses potential spatial bias by removing duplicate points and uses a comprehensive set of environmental variables.

results.result: Migration analyses revealed asymmetrical gene flow patterns in septentrional East Asia, with symmetrical moderate gene flow between the northeastern mainland and Korean Peninsula (M1-3=0.106, M3-1=0.214), but asymmetrical flow toward the Amur River Basin (higher inflow, lower outflow), and negligible symmetrical flow between B. stejnegeri subpopulations in Korea.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C117 present migration rate estimates using MIGRATE with appropriate parameters (unlinked loci, multiple independent runs, MCMC convergence assessment). The migration rates are quantified with specific values (Supplementary file 1H, Figure 8) and theta estimates. The patterns are clearly described and visualized. However, the analysis could benefit from confidence intervals or credible intervals for the migration rate estimates, and more explicit discussion of the statistical significance of the asymmetry.

results.result: Species delimitation using Bayes Factor Delimitation identified Model A as the best-supported scenario (MLE: -502.801, Bayes factor: 3.198), supporting the split of East Asian Bufo into seven independent taxonomic units: B. j. japonicus, B. j. formosus, B. andrewsi, B. gargarizans, B. stejnegeri, B. bankorensis, and B. sachalinensis, with species-level boundaries between Japanese Bufo subspecies and merging of Korean and Amur River Basin clades under B. sachalinensis.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C124 present a rigorous species delimitation analysis using coalescent-based BFD methods with path sampling to compare eight alternative models (Supplementary file 1I, Figure 9). Model A received the highest support with a positive Bayes factor (3.198), indicating it is favored over alternative models. The analysis includes appropriate MCMC diagnostics (ESS >200) and tests multiple biologically relevant scenarios. The results are consistent with other lines of evidence (phylogenetic, ecological, biogeographic). The Bayes factor value is relatively modest, suggesting some uncertainty, but the model selection framework is sound.

results.result: The study validated B. andrewsi as a distinct species, rejecting previous synonymization with B. gargarizans. This conclusion is supported by species delimitation analysis (Model A), polyphyletic mtDNA structure, independent evolutionary lineage in the multilocus tree, morphometric data, and divergence timing associated with QTP orogenesis during the Late Miocene.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 and C187-C190 present multiple lines of evidence supporting B. andrewsi as a distinct species: (1) species delimitation analysis (Figure 9), (2) phylogenetic evidence (Figures 4, 5), (3) morphometric data from Liao et al., 2016, and (4) biogeographic evidence (Table 3, Figure 5). The integration of molecular, morphological, and biogeographic data provides strong support for this taxonomic revision. The rejection of previous synonymization (Fu et al., 2005) is well-justified.

results.result: The study validated B. bankorensis as an independent species, supported by polyphyletic mtDNA structure, independent evolutionary lineage in the multilocus BFD tree, species delimitation analysis, contemporaneous divergence time with other B. gargarizans complex clades during the Mid to Late Pleistocene, and elevation-related niche segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C127 and C196-C199 present multiple lines of evidence supporting B. bankorensis as a distinct species: (1) phylogenetic evidence showing polyphyletic structure in mtDNA (Figures 4B, 5) and independent lineage in multilocus tree (Figure 9), (2) species delimitation analysis (Figure 9), (3) dating analysis showing divergence during glaciation period (Figure 5), and (4) ecological evidence of elevation-related niche segregation (Lin and Lue, 2004; Fu et al., 2005). The integration of molecular, temporal, and ecological data provides strong support for this taxonomic revision, rejecting previous synonymization (Liu et al., 2000).

results.result: The study elevated the septentrional East Asia clade to species level as Bufo sachalinensis (originally described as B. vulgaris sachalinensis Nikolsky, 1905), with two subspecies: B. s. sachalinensis in the Amur River Basin and B. s. cf. sachalinensis on the Korean Peninsula. This taxonomic revision is supported by species delimitation analysis, Middle Pleistocene divergence, ecological niche segregation, population expansion from LGM, and gene flow patterns toward northern latitudes.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132, C139-C140, C191-C193, and C210-C212 present the major taxonomic revision of the study, elevating B. sachalinensis to species level. This is supported by: (1) species delimitation analysis (Model A; Figure 9), (2) dating analysis showing Middle Pleistocene divergence (Figure 5), (3) ecological niche modeling showing significant segregation from B. gargarizans (Figure 7), (4) population dynamics showing LGM expansion (Figure 6), (5) migration analysis showing gene flow patterns (Figure 8), and (6) phylogenetic evidence from both mtDNA and nuDNA (Figure 4). The integration of multiple independent lines of evidence provides strong support for this taxonomic revision. The assignment to subspecies reflects geographic and genetic distinction. The use of the historical name B. vulgaris sachalinensis Nikolsky, 1905 follows nomenclatural priority.

results.result: The study demonstrated that the combined impacts of long dispersal and ice-age refugia equally contributed to the current genetic structure of Bufo in East Asia, rejecting the dominance of any single phylogeographic hypothesis. This is supported by deeper segregation around the Yellow Sea visible in both mtDNA and nuDNA, population expansion in septentrional East Asia related to LGM, and synchrony with the Sanduo Event that widened the Yellow Sea basin.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C135-C136, and C167-C172 present a synthesis of phylogeographic results that integrates multiple lines of evidence: (1) phylogenetic evidence showing segregation around the Yellow Sea in both mtDNA and nuDNA (Figure 4, Figure 6), (2) population dynamics showing expansion in septentrional East Asia but not in B. gargarizans (Figure 6), (3) dating analysis showing timing consistent with geological events (Lei et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016), and (4) comparison with other amphibian clades (Borzée et al., 2020). The conclusion that multiple factors contributed equally is well-supported by the data, though 'equally' may be somewhat imprecise. The rejection of the long dispersal hypothesis (Zhan and Fu, 2011) is justified by the evidence for refugia and vicariance.

results.result: Climate-driven adaptation in septentrional Eastern Asian Bufo (B. sachalinensis) explains its range shifts toward northern latitudes, supported by niche segregation based on minimum temperatures, low gene flow rates indicating genetic drift and local adaptation, weak impact of long-distance dispersal in the Amur River Basin, and reduced dispersal capacity compensating for energy investment in low-temperature tolerance.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C138, and C173-C180 present evidence for climate-driven adaptation in B. sachalinensis: (1) ecological niche modeling showing temperature-based segregation (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), (2) migration analysis showing low gene flow rates (Figure 8), (3) population dynamics showing expansion in northern latitudes (Figure 6), and (4) discussion of trade-offs between dispersal and cold tolerance (Kolbe et al., 2010). The integration of ecological, genetic, and demographic data provides strong support for local adaptation. However, the claim of 'climate-driven adaptation' is somewhat inferential, as direct evidence of adaptive genetic changes (e.g., selection scans, functional studies) is not provided. The evidence is consistent with adaptation but does not definitively prove it.

results.result: STRUCTURE analysis of nuclear data (POMC-RAG-1-Rho) identified two genetic clusters (K=2) within East Asian Bufo: the first cluster included populations from western, central, southeastern, and northeastern Asian mainland along with Japanese Bufo; the second cluster was restricted to B. sachalinensis of septentrional East Asia (Korean Peninsula, Amur River Basin, Sakhalin Island) and B. bankorensis from Taiwan Island.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 present STRUCTURE analysis results with appropriate statistical measures (Mean LnProb=-827.838, mean similarity score=0.974) indicating good convergence across runs. The identification of K=2 as the optimal number of clusters is supported by the data (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 1F). The cluster assignments are consistent with phylogenetic and species delimitation results. The presence of admixture in central and southeastern mainland Asia is noted and consistent with the study's discussion of introgression and trade impacts.

results.result: The study refined divergence times for Neotropical and Eurasian bufonid lineages using fossil calibrations, rejecting the hypothesis of shared origin and confirming dispersion from Europe into East Asia. The emergence of bufonids into Europe was subsequent to the Eurasia-Africa landmass connection, and the Miocene radiations within Western Palearctic Bufo (c. 14.49-11.03 Mya) are consistent with the highest dusting outflow in Central Asian deserts (c. 15.00-13.00 Mya).
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C146 present biogeographic interpretations based on the dating analysis (Table 1, Figure 2) and ancestral range reconstruction. The rejection of the African origin hypothesis (Sanchiz, 1997) and the East Asia to Europe dispersal hypothesis (Sanchiz, 1997; Roček and Rage, 2003) is supported by the time estimates and ancestral range analysis. The confirmation of Europe to East Asia dispersal is consistent with Garcia-Porta et al., 2012. The temporal correlation with Central Asian desertification (Guo et al., 2002) is well-supported. The speculation about early colonization prior to the second dusting period (C146) is appropriately qualified as 'may have.'

results.result: The study detected loss of genetic structure within B. gargarizans clades, possibly due to introgression resulting from traditional medicine trade over a millennium. Evidence includes admixed individuals within B. gargarizans range showing high admixture with B. sachalinensis (95% and 87%), and gene flow patterns potentially revealing directionality of trade rather than natural dispersal.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C184 and C137 present an interpretation of genetic patterns as resulting from human-mediated trade. While the presence of admixed individuals (Supplementary file 1F, Figure 4D) and loss of genetic structure are documented, the attribution to trade is largely inferential. The citations to Zhan et al., 2020 and Lee et al., 2021 support the historical context of trade, but direct evidence linking the observed genetic patterns specifically to trade (rather than natural dispersal or other factors) is limited. The interpretation is plausible and consistent with the data, but alternative explanations (e.g., natural secondary contact, incomplete lineage sorting) are not fully ruled out. The claim would be strengthened by additional evidence such as genetic signatures of recent admixture, comparison with trade routes, or analysis of market samples.

results.result: Despite evidence supporting the splitting of B. j. formosus and B. j. japonicus based on Pliocene-Pleistocene divergence and species delimitation analysis, the study does not recommend further taxonomic changes because the taxonomy is already resolved, though the evidence could support future elevation to species level.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C201 present a conservative taxonomic recommendation. The evidence for independent evolution of the two subspecies is documented (Figures 5 and 9), but the authors appropriately defer to existing taxonomic resolution (Dubois and Bour, 2010; Matsui, 1984) and note the lack of a restricted type locality. This is a reasonable approach that acknowledges the evidence while respecting nomenclatural stability. The statement that the evidence 'could be used' for future elevation is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The study highlights conservation concerns for Bufo species, particularly risks from anthropogenic introductions (e.g., B. j. formosus introgression with B. j. japonicus, introduction on Hokkaido, pathogen spread), declining effective population size in Korean populations, and calls for limiting trade to regions within the geographic occurrence of each clade and genetic preservation of Asian Bufo clades.
results.evaluation: Claims C202-C205 and C214 present conservation recommendations based on the study's findings. The risks from anthropogenic introductions are documented with citations (Hase et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2020; Borzée et al., 2021). The declining effective population size in Korean populations is shown in Figure 6. The low genetic variability in B. s. cf. sachalinensis (π=4.76±2.34; Supplementary file 1D) is documented. The conservation recommendations are appropriate and well-justified by the data. These are important practical implications of the taxonomic and phylogeographic findings.

results.result: The study concludes that past paleogeological events (Central Asian desertification, QTP orogenesis, Japanese continental drift) have been the most powerful factors promoting genetic structures of Bufo in the Eastern Palearctic since the Miocene, with co-distribution and artificial secondary contact resulting in blurry genetic structure in central East Asian lowlands, and glaciations impacting range expansions and leading to microclimate adaptation along latitudinal gradients.
results.evaluation: Claims C206-C209 present a synthesis of the study's major findings. The conclusion that paleogeological events were the most powerful factors is supported by the model selection analysis (C153, Supplementary file 1C, Figure 3) showing geological events had higher likelihood than other factors. The evidence for blurry genetic structure in B. gargarizans (C208) is supported by the phylogenetic discordance (Figure 4) and discussion of introgression and trade. The impact of glaciations on range expansions (C209) is supported by population dynamics (Figure 6) and dating analyses (Figure 5). This is an appropriate high-level summary of the study's contributions.
